answer.summary: Yes for the live full-jitter scheduler under test. Fifty catalog-policy runs (base=2.0s, cap=60.0s, attempts=3, timeout=3600.0s) produced 50 distinct interval tuples; two explicit runs differed; every sampled sum was strictly below timeout. An exhaustive cartesian check over 2300 (base, cap, attempts, timeout) cells proved the clip construction keeps sum < timeout, including 350 cells where the unclipped exponential worst-case meets or exceeds timeout (tight fixture unclipped=180.0s vs timeout=50s). A fixed-interval unjittered implementation produces identical interval sets across runs and therefore fails the non-determinism assertion.

sut.algorithm: AWS full jitter: delay=Uniform(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt))
sut.bound: each delay clipped to remaining_timeout - eps so sum(schedule) < timeout_seconds

symbolic.proof: delay_i = min(Uniform(0, ceiling_i), remaining_i - eps); remaining_{i+1} = timeout - sum(delay_0..delay_i); by induction sum < timeout for every attempt count in range. Unclipped worst-case = sum_i min(cap, base*2^i) and is allowed to exceed timeout; clipping is then load-bearing.
